metadata.title: The causes and consequences of field-of-study mismatch (EN)

survey_design.weight_variable_name: final weight (PIAAC full final weight; jackknife replicate weights via PIAAC Tool macro)
survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PIAAC’s probability-sampling design and applies jackknife replicate weights to obtain design-correct standard errors, implemented through the publicly available SAS/Stata “PIAAC Tool” macro. The analytic sample is restricted to employed workers aged 15–64 in fields other than “general programmes”, excluding self-employed and other ineligible occupation groups, and further excludes wage outliers (below the 1st and above the 99th percentile within each country). For country-specific analyses, estimates are weighted using the full final weight; for pooled analyses, weights are adjusted so each country contributes an equal weighted sum of observations (targeting an average country sample size) to prevent large countries from dominating. Missing values on analytical variables are imputed to the country-specific mean using a dummy-variable imputation approach (Allison, 2002), after which the weighted, replicate-weighted estimation is performed.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This document is an official IEA/OECD technical report or assessment framework. It describes sampling, scaling, and instrument design rather than student-level predictive modeling. Plausible values are therefore not applicable to the document's primary analytic purpose; any missing-data discussion refers to fieldwork or scaling procedures, not a single ML imputation strategy.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The full PIAAC sample contains 165,599 observations. The analysis excludes respondents whose field-of-study is “general programmes” (n=25,303), excludes ISCO-08 major group 0 (armed forces) and other unclassifiable occupations (n=960 and n=13,987), and excludes cases where field-of-study mismatch cannot be determined due to missing occupation (n=58,289) or missing field-of-study (n=40,505). For analyses of mismatch likelihood, job satisfaction, and wages, the study further excludes self-employed or not-employed individuals. Wage regressions exclude observations with wages outside the 1st–99th percentile within each country. For pooled models using system-level covariates, the Russian Federation is excluded due to missing country-level macro-economic factor data, and certain older workers are excluded where labour-market indicators are unavailable for the year they began their job.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD analysis uses PIAAC 2012 Adult Skills microdata to quantify field-of-study mismatch and to estimate how labour-demand (field saturation) and labour-supply (skill transferability) relate to mismatch, then evaluates individual and national costs. The study applies PIAAC’s complex survey design using jackknife replicate weights and uses plausible values for literacy/numeracy-based measures where appropriate. Across pooled models, field saturation is a robust predictor of mismatch: a one-standard-deviation increase in saturation raises the odds of mismatch by about 64%, while skill transferability shows weak or context-dependent pooled effects. For consequences, the wage penalty is small when qualifications are adequate (~3%) but large when mismatch coincides with overqualification (~25%), and mismatch is associated with higher unemployment/out-of-labour-force risk (18.1% vs 13.4%). Limitations include reliance on observational, cross-sectional associations and the use of imputation for missing analytical variables, so causal claims cannot be inferred.
